I checked the whole CRM, not just a search: `search_context`'s meaning-based lane isn't indexed in this workspace, so I enumerated the activity corpus directly. That came back `complete_exact` — **six activities in total since 2024, four of which are about this exact topic.** So what follows is everything the CRM holds, not a sample.

## Yes — it happened at three accounts

| When | Account | What was recorded |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-09-18 | Reply Deutschland | Inbound email from **Katrin Sommer**, subject *"Wechsel der Ansprechpartner"*: „Der ständige Wechsel der Ansprechpartner ist für uns ein echtes Problem." |
| 2025-11-04 | valantic AG | Inbound email: „Nach dem Wechsel des Ansprechpartners kam fünf Tage lang keine Antwort." |
| 2025-11-04 | Körber Digital | Inbound email, **word-for-word the same sentence** as valantic |
| 2025-12-03 | Reply Deutschland | Internal note, *"Post-mortem Betreuerwechsel"*: „Der Kunde hat das im Oktober klar angesprochen; wir haben zu spät reagiert." |

## What actually happened, and how we reacted

Two different complaints are mixed together here, and only one of them is about swapping people too often:

- **Reply Deutschland** complained about the *frequency* — "ständige" (constant) — i.e. the pattern across time.
- **valantic and Körber** complained about a *responsiveness gap*: five days of silence immediately after the handover. Same phrasing at both, three weeks apart. That is the concrete failure mode, and it is not really about how often you switch — it is about the switch being unstaffed for a week.

**How we reacted: as far as the CRM records, we didn't.** There is no outbound reply logged against any of the three complaints, no task, no commitment, no deal, no owner-change entry. The only response on record is the post-mortem two and a half months after the first complaint, and it says so itself: „wir haben zu spät reagiert."

One thing worth chasing offline: the post-mortem says the customer raised it **in October**, but the only Reply complaint on file is dated **18 September**. Either there was an October escalation nobody logged, or the post-mortem is recalling the date loosely. Either way, the escalation the post-mortem is actually about is not in this system.

## What to prepare for

1. **The complaint arrives within about five days.** That is the observed window at both accounts that quantified it. Your risk period is the first week, not the first quarter.
2. **The trigger is silence, not the change itself.** Nobody complained about *who* took over. They complained that mail went unanswered while the seat was empty.
3. **It compounds.** Reply's wording ("constant") means they were counting. If this account has been switched before, expect a sharper reaction than the raw history suggests.
4. **It will likely be raised by email, in writing, to whoever is nominally on the account** — all three landed as inbound mail, which means it will sit unread if the new manager isn't monitoring the old inbox from day one.

## What we can learn

- **Cover the first week explicitly.** The old manager stays reachable and on the thread for at least the five days that burned us twice. A dated handover note in the CRM, not a verbal one.
- **Announce before they discover it.** In all three cases the customer told us; we never told them first.
- **Log the reaction.** The post-mortem's whole finding was slow reaction, and yet the CRM cannot show what we eventually did — so we can't tell you today whether the fix worked. Whatever you do this time, put it on the record so the next person has more than four emails to go on.
- **Watch Reply Deutschland in particular** if it is on your list, since they are the account already primed on this.

## Two caveats you should weigh

**The evidence base is thin, and the records look staged.** All three of these organizations are literally named "*<Company>* Betreuerwechsel", carry `lifecycle: unknown`, `classification: prospect`, have no deals attached, and two have no contacts at all. These read more like scenario or test records than live customer accounts. The complaints are real text in the system, but I would not present them to anyone as documented customer history without confirming their provenance first.

**The CRM cannot tell you who took over from whom.** There is no owner-change history and the workspace has one human seat, so the "who" side of every past handover is not recoverable here.

You didn't say which account you're about to change. If you tell me, I'll check whether it has any of this history of its own and what coverage it currently rests on — and I can draft the handover note and the first-week follow-up task if that's useful. Nothing is waiting in the approval queue; I only read, and changed nothing.
